title: Module 5 — Active Directory, accounts, and Microsoft 365

spans.text: [VISUAL/DIAGRAM SUGGESTION: A Windows domain with DC/DNS, joined PCs, Group Policy, and an Outlook profile.]

Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) centrally manages domain users, computers, and groups. A Domain Controller (DC) provides authentication and directory queries and often runs DNS. Common ports include Kerberos TCP/UDP 88, LDAP TCP/UDP 389, LDAPS TCP 636, DNS TCP/UDP 53, and SMB TCP 445. Do not open these indiscriminately; use approved rules within managed networks.

Before joining, a PC needs access to the organization network and correct internal DNS, a reasonable clock, and a unique name. Start from Settings > System > About > Domain or workgroup (or the organization’s enrollment method); authorized domain credentials may be required. If it fails, check DC discovery through DNS, time difference, VPN/LAN connectivity, and account rights. A workgroup is not a domain; do not unjoin a device without approval.

At onboarding, create a unique identity, follow approved naming, grant only required group membership, and deliver an initial credential securely. Review and remove unneeded access when a role changes. At departure, disable the account at the approved time, revoke active sessions/tokens, and transfer devices and data ownership according to policy. Support password and MFA recovery, but never ask for or share a password.

Group Policy (GPO) applies consistent security and work settings to domain users and devices. GPOs apply according to OU (Organizational Unit) scope and link order; inspect results with `gpresult /r` or `gpresult /h report.html`. `gpupdate /force` requests refresh, but not every setting changes immediately; some policies need sign-out or reboot. For issues, review scope, Security Filtering, inheritance, and recent changes, using approved change procedures.

A Microsoft 365 account is a cloud identity that may be synchronized with on-premises AD, but do not assume identical passwords or lifecycle by default. Licensing, MFA, and conditional access follow organization policy. Outlook/Exchange Online uses Autodiscover and HTTPS-based services; client traffic commonly uses TCP 443. For sign-in issues, check account state, assigned license, MFA method, and service health; never ask someone else to approve an MFA prompt for you.

An OST is a synchronized local cache for an Exchange/Microsoft 365 mailbox. A PST is an export/archive file and should be protected as data; do not mistake an OST for an archive or a PST for a server mailbox. For OST trouble, close Outlook, check connectivity and mailbox quota, and only consider rebuilding it under guidance with a backup. If a PST will not open, check permissions, disk space, size, and backup; run `scanpst.exe` on a copy. Get the data owner’s approval before moving or deleting files.

Ask for the exact error, scope, and recent changes, and record the time. Compare with Outlook on the web or another approved device, but do not forward confidential mail to a personal channel. Check Microsoft 365 service health, network/VPN, DNS, license, and profile in sequence. Deleting a profile, changing OST/PST files, or reconnecting an account may cause data loss or downtime; obtain authorization, backup, and change approval first.

Kerberos requires client and DC clocks to be aligned; a large difference can prevent ticket issuance. For sign-in errors, check time zone, synchronization, internal DNS, and VPN/LAN access. Use the organization’s time source, not a random NTP server. A new sign-in or GPO refresh may be needed after correction.

spans.code:
User -> DNS -> DC (Kerberos/88) -> groups and GPO
PC -> domain | Outlook -> Microsoft 365 (HTTPS/443)
OST = synchronized cache | PST = export/archive file
